passage:
Sonali, you asked why I deleted my "goals" folder. So, I'm Mehak, and for six months I followed all these gym and makeup creators, and every morning I felt I had to change something: my hair, my stomach, my skin. I bought things I didn't need.
Then one night I watched one of them pitch a "transformation plan", her discount code flashing in the same breath as telling us how much we needed fixing. I thought: who earns when I feel inadequate? She does.
So I unfollowed most of them. Now I follow a swimming coach who posts drills and a science teacher who explains how things work. My mornings are quieter. I still notice myself comparing sometimes, but now I ask who is selling what.

qa.q: What flashed on screen with the influencer's transformation plan?
qa.a: Her discount code flashed on screen in the same breath as the plan.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling every morning while following the influencers?
qa.a: She felt she had to change something, like her hair, stomach or skin, which suggests envy and a sense of not being enough.

qa.q: What did Mehak change about whom she follows, and why?
qa.a: She unfollowed most of them after asking who earns when she feels inadequate, and now picks accounts that teach real things. 😊

qa.q: How might the influencer see her transformation plan?
qa.a: She may see it as a product and her followers as customers, so she benefits when viewers feel they need fixing.

grounding: Shows a teen envying fitness and beauty influencers, asking who benefits from her inadequacy and choosing accounts for evidence and wellbeing.

passage:
Sit, Kashish. I'm your Nirmala Masi, and I'm going to tell you about the year your sister Avni got trapped in her own head. She counted every bite on her phone and checked the mirror each time she passed it. Food felt like something she couldn't manage, and it frightened her.
I didn't tell her to just eat. I told her this was a reason to talk to somebody early. She was afraid I'd be angry, but the next day I took her to the family doctor, and she said it all out loud, which took more courage than anything else that year.
It isn't weakness to ask for help, beta. She is still working on it, with people beside her.

qa.q: Whom did Nirmala Masi take Avni to see?
qa.a: She took Avni to the family doctor.

qa.q: How did Avni feel about food, and about telling anyone?
qa.a: Food felt like something she couldn't manage, which frightened her, and she was afraid Masi would be angry.

qa.q: What did Masi do that helped Avni?
qa.a: Masi didn't tell her to just eat; she took her to the family doctor the next day, so Avni could say it all out loud.

qa.q: Why does Masi tell Kashish this story?
qa.a: Masi wants Kashish to know that asking for help early is a strength, and that Kashish's sister was not alone.

grounding: Shows a teen who counts food and checks mirrors constantly feeling frightened, and an elder steering her to a doctor early.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10.
Lavanya told me that her mother, Sarika, often says at dinner that she should "watch what she eats" and try a fairness cream "so people notice you". Lavanya knows it comes from love, but it stings, and she goes quiet at the table.
We practised a sentence together: "Amma, when you say that, I feel small. Can we talk about being healthy together instead?" She wrote it on her palm.
A week later she told me she had said it. Sarika went quiet, then suggested evening walks together. Lavanya says they still slip, but her mother now says, "Sorry, old habit." I will see them both next month if they wish.

qa.q: What did Sarika suggest after Lavanya spoke up?
qa.a: Sarika suggested evening walks together.

qa.q: Why does Lavanya go quiet at the table even though she knows her mother means well?
qa.a: The comments sting and make her feel small, even though she knows they come from love.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Lavanya do?
qa.a: The counsellor helped her practise saying how the comments feel, ask for kinder words and suggest healthy habits together.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt on hearing that Lavanya feels small?
qa.a: Sarika went quiet, which suggests surprise and maybe regret, since she meant well and hadn't seen the sting.

grounding: Shows a teen stung by a parent's well-meant comments on weight and complexion, saying how it feels and proposing shared health habits.

passage:
Sunday, late. Today I told Hansa I hate my ears and the way my voice cracks. She said, "You look fine, honestly," and I nearly rolled my eyes. Then she told me she hides her forehead under her fringe every single day and hates how loudly she laughs. I'd never noticed either thing.
I realised I'd been carrying my worries around like they were only mine. We ended up laughing about our "flaws club" until Amma knocked to say lights out.
I'm still not sure my ears are fine, but I believe Hansa cares. Tomorrow I'll ask her about the science project instead of our faces.
Santosh

qa.q: What does Hansa hide under her fringe?
qa.a: She hides her forehead.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after Hansa shared her own insecurities?
qa.a: Santosh felt less alone, having realised the worries weren't only theirs to carry. 🙂

qa.q: How can Santosh support Hansa back without attaching worth to looks?
qa.a: Santosh can listen, share honestly and turn to shared interests like the science project instead of ranking faces.

qa.q: Why might Hansa have shared her own insecurities?
qa.a: Hansa may have wanted Santosh to know they weren't alone, which made "you look fine" feel honest instead of just polite.

grounding: Shows a teen feeling less alone when a friend reassures and shares her own insecurities.

passage:
In the narrow bathroom of the family flat in Delhi, Jagdish pulled on his school shirt and thought, my stomach looks weird today. He stopped. What would he say if Preeti said this out loud? Probably, "You're fine, and we're late for chai."
So he said the same to himself, quietly, and left.
It was a bad body day, not a bad life. At the canteen Preeti waved him to the last free bench. "Rehearsal at four, don't forget." He hadn't thought of skipping it, and he didn't love his body that morning, but he didn't need to. Neutral was enough. He sat down with his tea and went to rehearsal later in his crumpled shirt.

qa.q: What time was the rehearsal?
qa.a: The rehearsal was at four.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel about his body that morning, and what changed when he imagined Preeti saying the same words?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious about his stomach, but realising he would tell Preeti she was fine showed him how unkind he was being, and he settled into feeling neutral, which was enough.

qa.q: How did Jagdish treat the bad body day?
qa.a: He spoke to himself as he would to a friend, called it a bad body day, not a bad life, and carried on with his plans without needing to love his body. 🙂

qa.q: How might Preeti see Jagdish arriving in a crumpled shirt?
qa.a: Preeti probably just sees a friend showing up for rehearsal, and doesn't notice the shirt or the stomach at all.

grounding: Shows a teen on a bad body day speaking to himself as to a friend and going on with his plans.

passage:
In the changing room at school in Chennai, Karthik noticed how tall the boys from 9B already were, how deep their voices sounded, while his own stayed high. He compared his chin with theirs, his shoulders too.
Sabina, from the flat next door, met him at the lift holding her cricket bat. "You look like you swallowed a lemon."
"Everyone's growing except me."
"My cousin was shorter than me until last year, and now he's taller than his dad," she said. "Everybody's on a different clock."
Karthik gave a half laugh. That night he read the chapter on adolescence in his science book, ate a proper dinner and went to bed on time. "Not a race," he told the ceiling.

qa.q: What was Sabina holding when she met Karthik at the lift?
qa.a: She was holding her cricket bat.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he compared himself with the boys from 9B?
qa.a: He felt behind and self-conscious, comparing his chin, shoulders and voice, and told Sabina everyone was growing except him.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that shows patience and care for himself?
qa.a: He read about adolescence in his science book, ate a proper dinner, went to bed on time and reminded himself it is not a race. 😊

qa.q: How does Sabina see Karthik's worry?
qa.a: Sabina sees it as a common worry and reassures him with her cousin's example that bodies grow on different clocks, without mocking.

grounding: Shows a teen comparing his puberty with others' and learning that bodies develop at different speeds.

passage:
At his new school in Johannesburg, Siddiq began copying how the football crowd talked, dropping his mother's language on the phone, wearing the same low-slung jeans and laughing at jokes he didn't get. On Friday he skipped chess club, because it wasn't cool.
Thabo caught up with him at the gate. "You're doing an impression of somebody."
Siddiq shrugged, then admitted it. "I just want them to like me."
"Fine. Wear the jeans, learn the slang. But I liked you when you were explaining the Sicilian defence."
That weekend Siddiq still hung out with the football group, but he brought a chess board along, and wore what he wanted. Two boys asked to play.

qa.q: Which club did Siddiq skip on Friday?
qa.a: He skipped chess club.

qa.q: How did Siddiq feel at his new school, and what did he do about it?
qa.a: He felt insecure and anxious to be liked, admitting "I just want them to like me", so he copied the football crowd's talk and clothes.

qa.q: How did Siddiq balance fitting in with staying himself?
qa.a: He kept some of the group's style but brought his chess board and wore what he wanted, so he adapted lightly and kept his core.

qa.q: How does Thabo see Siddiq's change?
qa.a: Thabo sees a friend doing an impression of somebody else, and reminds him that he was liked for who he was, chess included.

grounding: Shows a teen changing his talk and dress to fit in, and Thabo helping him keep his core.

passage:
Anjali, you asked why I went quiet last spring. I'm Elizabeth, and I couldn't sleep, because I didn't know what my feelings meant: who I liked, and how, and whether I should be afraid of the answer. I googled at two in the morning, which only made it noisier. I told myself I had to pick a word for it right now.
Then the school librarian noticed me standing at the shelf too long and said there's no deadline on labels. They handed me a book from a reliable youth organisation. And you didn't ask me anything, you just kept sitting with me at lunch.
The fear didn't vanish, but it got smaller. I'm still figuring it out, and I'm okay with that.

qa.q: At what time was Elizabeth googling?
qa.a: Elizabeth was googling at two in the morning.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth afraid of during that spring?
qa.a: Elizabeth was afraid of what the feelings meant and of the answer, and felt a label was needed right away.

qa.q: What helped Elizabeth feel less afraid?
qa.a: Elizabeth heard there is no deadline on labels, got reliable information from the librarian and had Anjali's quiet company at lunch.

qa.q: How might Anjali have seen those quiet lunches?
qa.a: Anjali showed acceptance by sitting with Elizabeth without asking questions, which helped Elizabeth feel safe.

grounding: Shows a teen unsure about who they are and their feelings of attraction, afraid, finding no deadline for labels, safe people and reliable information.

passage:
"Can I tell you something?" Vishal asked, gripping a mug in Rajni's kitchen.
"Anything."
"There's a part of me my family doesn't know. I've never said it out loud. Please don't tell anyone."
Rajni sat down opposite. "Okay. I'm listening."
Vishal said it, quietly, and then stared at the table.
"Thank you for trusting me," Rajni said. "Nothing changes between us. It's yours to tell, nobody else's."
Just then Rajni's mother walked in. "Pakoras, anyone?" Vishal stiffened. "We were doing maths," Rajni said smoothly, taking the plate.
Later, at the door, Vishal whispered, "Thanks." "Any time," said Rajni.

qa.q: What did Rajni's mother offer?
qa.a: Rajni's mother offered pakoras.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when Rajni's mother walked in?
qa.a: Vishal stiffened, afraid that the secret might be overheard or exposed.

qa.q: How did Rajni show being a safe person?
qa.a: Rajni listened, kept the confidence, said it was Vishal's to tell and smoothly covered when Rajni's mother came in.

qa.q: What might it have taken for Vishal to tell Rajni?
qa.a: It likely took courage and trust, since Vishal's family doesn't know and Vishal fears the truth being passed on.

grounding: Shows a friend trusted with a private truth about who they are, listening, keeping the confidence and not outing them.

passage:
The night before, Ada had told her family who she is. Her father had shouted, her brother had slammed a door, and her mother wouldn't look at her. Now Ada sat on the steps outside the community centre in Rotterdam with her knees pulled up, numb, as though something inside her had cracked.
Yosef, the youth worker, sat two steps below and said nothing for a while. Then he said, "That sounds like heartbreak. It says nothing about your worth."
He gave her the number of a support line and told her she was welcome here after school. "Take your time. You don't have to decide anything today. If home doesn't feel safe tonight, tell me." Ada nodded slowly, and held the number in her fist.

qa.q: What did Yosef give Ada?
qa.a: He gave her the number of a support line.

qa.q: What was Ada feeling on the steps outside the community centre?
qa.a: She felt numb and heartbroken, as though something inside her had cracked.

qa.q: What safe supports did Yosef offer Ada?
qa.a: He offered a support line number, a welcome at the community centre after school, time to decide, and help if home doesn't feel safe.

qa.q: How might Ada's family be feeling in the moment?
qa.a: The shouting, the slammed door and the averted eyes suggest shock or fear, though it hurts Ada, and their reaction does not decide her worth.

grounding: Shows a teen whose family reacts harshly to who she is, heartbroken, finding a safe supporter and a helpline.
